descriptor.assumptions: Mole fractions of elements are taken as proxies for available ionic charge (all Na+, K+ etc. counted as +1, alkaline earths as +2); Al is assumed to be the only framework charge source, ignoring B, Ga, Zn, Ge substitution and fluoride/OH-mediated defect charging, which is why the +0.001 offset and the simple ratio are only rough proxies. OSDA charge is assumed fully available for framework balancing and scaled by its gel mole fraction; neutral amines (charge 0) contribute nothing. Gels with Al = 0 collapse to a large ratio dominated by cations, which should read as 'alkali/F-dominated, OSDA or defect balancing' — a regime ambiguity the tree must resolve in combination with F and OH.
descriptor.expected_effect: As cation_charge_per_Al increases well above ~1, probability mass should shift toward low-silica alkali-directed frameworks (LTA, FAU, CHA, P/GIS) and toward Failed (amorphous or dense alkali silicates) for high-silica-leaning gels; as it approaches or drops below ~1 with a substantial OSDA fraction, outcomes should concentrate in high-silica OSDA-templated frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW, MWW, TON).
descriptor.falsification: If high-Si/Al OSDA-templated products (MFI, *BEA, MTW) are obtained with high cation-charge-to-Al ratios while low-silica frameworks appear at ratios near 1, or if the descriptor shows no split power beyond what Al and Na mole fractions alone already provide, the charge-balance competition hypothesis is contradicted for this dataset.
descriptor.hypothesis: The ratio of total available counter-cation charge (inorganic alkali/alkaline-earth cations plus the organic cation charge contributed by OSDA1, weighted by its gel fraction) to the gel aluminum content determines whether crystallization is steered toward alkali-templated low-silica frameworks, OSDA-templated high-silica frameworks, or failure. When available cation charge greatly exceeds what is needed to balance framework Al (ratio >> 1), excess alkali dominates structure direction and favors small-pore, low-silica, alkali-stabilized frameworks (LTA, FAU, CHA, GIS-type P, dense phases) or keeps the gel amorphous; when the ratio is near or below the charge-balance requirement, OSDA-mediated charge ordering around framework Al/defect sites controls nucleation, favoring high-silica OSDA-directed topologies (MFI, *BEA/BEC, MTW, MWW, TON) whose formation requires a close match between OSDA charge and framework negative charge.
descriptor.mechanism: Framework Al (and silicate defects in all-silica syntheses) generate anionic charge that must be compensated by cations; both NMR studies of as-made zeolites and charge-density-mismatch arguments show that the identity and amount of charge-compensating species (Na+ vs OSDA+) determine which host-guest charge-ordering motif is feasible, and therefore which framework nucleates. Alkali cations stabilize small rings (4-, 6-, 8-MR) around cation sites in low-silica frameworks, while bulky OSDAs must be charge-balanced 1:1 with Al or defects, restricting the accessible Si/Al window. The descriptor proxies this competition: a high surplus of inorganic cation charge relative to Al signals an alkali-dominated regime, while a ratio near 1 (or below, indicating F- or OH-mediated defect charge balancing in all-silica gels) signals an OSDA-dominated regime. The narrow composition windows reported for OSDA/alkali co-templated phases (e.g., P1/SUZ-4 with diquat + K+) are exactly captured by where this ratio sits relative to unity.

descriptor.assumptions: The formula assumes all gel fluoride is present as F- (or HF) and that sda1 multiplied by the formal OSDA charge approximates the available organic cation equivalents; it ignores fluoride consumption by glass/metal species and treats OH as irrelevant to this ratio. When sda1 = 0 (no OSDA) the descriptor collapses to a large value for any fluoride-bearing gel, so fluoride-only syntheses are lumped into the excess-fluoride regime; when both F and OSDA are 0 the descriptor is 0. It is a gel-composition proxy, not a measurement of actual HF/OSDA in solution.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the descriptor increases from 0: hydroxide-route outcomes (alkali-templated low-silica frameworks such as FAU/LTA/MOR, or amorphous/dense Failed products in OSDA-rich gels) should dominate; near 1: classic fluoride-route high-silica phases (*BEA, BEC, MTW, MFI, TON) should peak; above ~2: small-pore F-occluding frameworks (CHA, LEV, AST-type) and pure-silica products should become more frequent, with Failed also rising when fluoride excess prevents heteroatom incorporation entirely.
descriptor.falsification: If the descriptor carries no phase-selective information, adding it will not improve held-out-publication accuracy, or splits on it will not separate hydroxide-route, stoichiometric-fluoride, and excess-fluoride regimes; equivalently, if phase outcomes are statistically independent of F/(OSDA charge) within fixed Si/Al and cation levels, the hypothesis is contradicted.
descriptor.hypothesis: The molar amount of fluoride per unit of OSDA cation charge (the HF/OSDA ratio written in gel mole fractions) is a primary axis of phase selectivity that the model cannot currently reconstruct from single columns: gels with F_per_osda_charge near 0 are effectively hydroxide-route syntheses, gels near 1 follow the classic stoichiometric fluoride route, and gels with excess fluoride (>1-2) are pushed into a distinct fluoride-rich regime. Because tree ensembles split on one column at a time, this ratio must be provided explicitly.
descriptor.mechanism: Fluoride mineralizes silica at near-neutral pH, producing less polymerized, more crystalline frameworks than hydroxide media, and F- is frequently occluded in small cages or double-4-ring (D4R) units, stabilizing frameworks whose building units can host F- (e.g., CHA, AST, LTA, and Ge-containing BEC). When F- is roughly stoichiometric with OSDA cation charge (ratio ~1), the classic fluoride route dominates, favoring high-silica OSDA-directed phases such as *BEA/BEC, MTW, and MFI-type products. When fluoride is in large excess over the OSDA charge, F- can no longer be paired with OSDA; it competes with trivalent heteroatom (Al, B, Ga) incorporation into the framework and with hydroxide-controlled pathways, steering toward small-pore F-occluding frameworks, pure-silica variants, or no crystallization at all. When fluoride is absent or far below the OSDA charge, the gel behaves as a hydroxide-route synthesis, favoring alkali-assisted low-silica phases and dense by-products. Evidence [2] shows pure-silica phase selection (beta vs ZSM-5 vs amorphous) flips as HF/OSDA is varied from 0.13 to 1.00; evidence [3] shows excess fluoride (HF/OSDA = 2.0) opens previously inaccessible small-pore phases (ERS-7, PST-21/22) while HF/OSDA <= 1.0 gives FER/RUT-type products.

descriptor.assumptions: The mole-fraction ratio H2O/(Si+Al+P+Ge) is a proxy for the conventional H2O/SiO2 or H2O/(SiO2+Al2O3) gel dilution ratios reported in papers; it ignores whether water was batched as solvent or partly consumed/removed (e.g., dry-gel or solvent-free routes are indistinguishable at extreme low values, which correctly tags them as 'concentrated'). Treating all T atoms as equally framework-relevant is a simplification (B, Ti, Zr, Sn gels are approximated by their Si content); the 0.001 constant makes pure-water-free or T-free records benign but arbitrary. Extreme values (solvent-free vs very dilute) span orders of magnitude, so tree models will use coarse splits rather than a linear response.
descriptor.expected_effect: As h2o_per_framework_tatom increases (more dilute gels), selection should shift from OSDA-directed open frameworks (*BEA, BEC, MWW) and 'Failed' outcomes toward denser frameworks (MTW, MFI, TON, FER) and alkali-stabilized small-pore or dense phases (LTA, FAU, CHA); very dilute gels should also raise the 'Failed' (amorphous) rate. In fluoride-route syntheses specifically, the *BEA-vs-MTW competition should flip from *BEA (concentrated) to MTW (dilute), matching the cited Ostwald ripening behavior.
descriptor.falsification: If, within a fixed OSDA and F regime, product phase frequencies are statistically independent of h2o_per_framework_tatom (i.e., the same framework is obtained across a wide H2O/T range while composition variables alone explain the splits), or if the observed dilution trend runs opposite to the densification direction (dilute gels giving more open frameworks), the hypothesis is contradicted.
descriptor.hypothesis: The gel dilution level, expressed as moles of water per mole of framework-forming T atoms (Si, Al, P, Ge), is an independent axis of phase selectivity that the model cannot reconstruct from the single H2O and Si columns: concentrated (low H2O/T) gels crystallize metastable, more open or defect-rich frameworks and often the OSDA-directed phase first, while dilute (high H2O/T) gels favor thermodynamically denser frameworks, alkali-stabilized small-pore phases, or dense/amorphous 'Failed' products.
descriptor.mechanism: Water sets the chemical potential of dissolved silicate/aluminate/phosphate species and hence the supersaturation at nucleation. At low water content, high supersaturation and restricted mobility favor kinetic nucleation of open, metastable frameworks (e.g., *BEA/BEC over MTW in the cited fluoride study) and strengthen OSDA-framework structure direction; at high water content, species are well solvated, nucleation is slower, and the thermodynamically denser phase wins (Ostwald ripening toward the higher-framework-density phase), or the gel stays amorphous because supersaturation never builds. Water also moderates OH- activity and cation hydration, shifting the balance between alkali-templated (LTA, FAU, CHA, GIS-type) and OSDA-templated (MFI, *BEA, MTW, MWW, TON) regimes. Tree ensembles split on one column at a time, so this H2O:T ratio must be supplied explicitly as a single column.
